title: MCP 2026-07-28: The Stateless Specification
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) publishes its largest specification revision since launch. A release candidate has been public since mid-May 2026, giving SDK maintainers and client implementers a roughly ten-week window to validate the changes against real workloads before the final spec ships. The headline change: **MCP's protocol core becomes stateless.**

This page builds on the MCP architecture covered in [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents) — read that first for the client/server/transport basics.

---

## The Core Change: No More Sessions

Prior MCP versions required an `initialize` handshake and a protocol-level session, identified by an `Mcp-Session-Id` header, that pinned a client to a specific server instance for the life of a connection. The 2026-07-28 revision removes both entirely:

- **No handshake.** Every request is now fully self-contained — a client can issue `tools/call` without a prior `initialize` round trip.
- **No session ID.** Any request can be served by any server instance, since no server-side session state is required to interpret it.

**Why it matters:** a remote MCP server that previously needed sticky sessions, a shared session store, and deep packet inspection at the load-balancer layer can now run behind a plain round-robin load balancer, route on an `Mcp-Method` header, and let clients cache `tools/list` responses for as long as the server's `ttlMs` value permits. This makes MCP servers dramatically simpler to scale horizontally.

---

## Extensions Framework

Statelessness pushed some existing functionality out of the protocol core and into a new **Extensions** mechanism — optional, independently versioned capabilities that a client and server negotiate support for. Two extensions ship with this revision:

### Tasks (SEP-2663)
Tasks shipped experimentally back in the 2025-11-25 spec as a core feature, but production use surfaced problems with a blocking `tasks/result` call. The redesign moves Tasks into a formal extension with a fully polling-based model:

- A server can respond to `tools/call` with a task handle instead of a result.
- The client drives progress with `tasks/get` (poll for status) and `tasks/update` (send additional input mid-task).
- Blocking `tasks/result` is gone; `tasks/list` was removed as unnecessary.

This is the same shape of problem Claude Code's own "long MCP calls move to background after 2 minutes" behavior solves client-side — see [Claude Code Overview](claude-code-overview).

### MCP Apps
MCP Apps let a server ship a sandboxed HTML-based UI that the host renders inside an iframe, rather than returning plain text or JSON for the client to format. This is aimed at MCP servers that benefit from richer, interactive output — dashboards, forms, visualizations — without every host needing bespoke rendering logic per server.

---

## Authorization Hardening

The revision aligns MCP's authorization flow more closely with standard OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect deployments, and promotes the **Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA)** extension to stable status. EMA gives organizations a centralized way to gate access to MCP servers through their existing identity provider, rather than each server implementing its own auth handling.

---

## Deprecation Policy

For the first time, MCP adopts a formal deprecation policy for protocol versions and fields, intended to give SDK authors and server operators predictable upgrade windows instead of ad hoc breaking changes.

---

## SDK Status

Beta releases supporting the 2026-07-28 revision are available across the major SDKs:

| SDK | Status |
|---|---|
| Python | v2 beta — `FastMCP` renamed to `MCPServer` |
| TypeScript | v2 beta — split into focused sub-packages |
| Go | v1.7.0-pre.1 — 2026-07-28 support |
| C# | 2.0.0-preview.1 |

---

## Practical Impact for Server Authors

Servers built against pre-2026-07-28 clients that rely on session pinning or the blocking `tasks/result` call will need updates once clients migrate. The ecosystem context: MCP passed 10,000+ published servers in 2026, so this migration touches a large existing base — expect a staged rollout rather than a hard cutover on July 28 itself.
